exam: Explain how a defect in the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase contributes to the clinical features of diabetic ketoacidosis.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Membrane transport moves substances across cell membranes via passive and active mechanisms, maintaining homeostasis and enabling drug action. Clinicians must recognise how transport defects cause disease and affect therapy.

b: Passive: follows concentration gradient, no energy.
Active: requires ATP or ion gradients.
sections.p: Cell membranes are lipid bilayers with proteins that allow selective movement of ions, nutrients, and waste. Transport can be passive (diffusion, facilitated diffusion) or active (primary, secondary).

b: Channel: pore, fast, voltage‑ or ligand‑gated.
Carrier: binds substrate, changes shape, slower.
sections.p: Understand the driving forces (concentration, electrical, electrochemical gradients) and the main transporter families (channels, carriers, pumps, exchangers).

t.b: Does the patient have a disturbance of ion gradients? Abnormal Na⁺/K⁺ suggests pump dysfunction or renal loss.
Is glucose transport impaired? Low glucose with normal insulin hints at GLUT‑1 deficiency.

b: Cystic fibrosis: CFTR channel defect → thick secretions, lung infection.
Diabetic ketoacidosis: Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase failure → cellular dehydration.
Malaria: parasite uses host GLUT1 to import glucose.
sections.p: Transport defects underlie many common disorders and influence drug absorption, distribution, and toxicity.

t.b: Is CFTR function abnormal? >60 mmol/L confirms cystic fibrosis.
Is anaerobic metabolism due to impaired oxidative transport? >2 mmol/L suggests tissue hypoxia.

b: Channel vs carrier defects produce different time courses.
Active transport requires ATP – think of energy‑dependent diseases.
sections.p: Focus on the link between transporter type and disease presentation, and on interpreting labs that reflect transport abnormalities.

b: Assuming normal labs mean normal transport – many values are compensatory.
Prescribing drugs that rely on a defective transporter.
sections.p: Students often list transport proteins without connecting to pathophysiology or ignore resource‑limited alternatives.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe electrolyte imbalance causing cardiac arrhythmia
Acute pulmonary edema from CFTR‑related lung failure
Rapidly worsening metabolic acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis
